To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the stochastic gradient algorithm with constant learning rate is the fastest among the considered methods for all problem sizes.
the sequence of function evaluations produced by stochastic gradient descent with momentum is deterministic, and the limiting neighborhood is described in terms of the eigenvectors of the Hessian.
the stochastic momentum method with optimal step-size converges to a neighborhood of the optimal point with radius of order 1/√n.
In summary, our research is concerned with
stochastic gradient algorithms for solving random least squares problems.
stochastic optimization algorithms for high-dimensional problems.
the analysis of stochastic optimization algorithms in the large-scale regime.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
, in the context of large-scale optimization, the use of stochastic gradient algorithms is a necessity, not a choice, and that momentum is an essential ingredient of such algorithms.

the stochastic momentum methods are the best choice for solving the random least squares problem, and they are nearly as efficient as the deterministic Newton method, which requires a matrix inversion and is therefore computationally intractable for large-scale problems.
The results of the present paper are a contribution to the study of the dynamics of stochastic gradient algorithms for solving random quadratic problems.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
, for the class of quadratic models, stochastic gradient algorithms with a momentum term have a simple and deterministic behavior, and the average-case complexity is nearly optimal.

we provide a deterministic characterization of stochastic gradient descent with momentum on a random least squares problem and use it to derive nearly-optimal hyperparameter settings and average-case complexity.
we have developed a new approach for analyzing stochastic gradient algorithms with momenta, and applied it to a high-dimensional quadratic optimization problem with random data.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the dynamics of stochastic momentum algorithms on large-scale problems can be understood in terms of the spectrum of the Hessian of the objective.

stochastic momentum methods, when applied to a quadratic objective with a random Hessian, exhibit a simple, deterministic dynamics that depends only on the spectrum of the Hessian and not on the particular realization of the Hessian.
the dynamics of stochastic gradient methods with momentum on large-scale, quadratic objectives is well-understood, and the optimal hyperparameter choices are surprisingly simple.
